title: Impact of Very-Low-Birth-Weight Classification on Neonatal Mortality

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy

**Method: Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD)**

This is a classic RDD setting. The very-low-birth-weight (VLBW) classification is determined by whether birth weight falls below a specific threshold (typically 1,500 grams, but here the running variable appears normalized/rescaled around a cutoff). The treatment — being classified as VLBW — is a deterministic function of the running variable (birth weight), creating a sharp discontinuity.

**Key Assumptions:**
1. **Continuity/No manipulation:** Parents and hospitals cannot precisely manipulate birth weight to fall just above or below the threshold (no bunching). Birth weight is essentially random in a narrow neighborhood of the cutoff.
2. **Local randomization:** Units just above and just below the threshold are comparable in all observable and unobservable characteristics, so any discontinuity in the outcome at the threshold is attributable to the VLBW classification.
3. **No other discontinuities:** No other policy or treatment changes discretely at the same threshold.

The running variable appears to be normalized so the cutoff is likely at 0.5 (given treated=0 for values around 0.4-0.5 and the `near_cutoff` variable). I will estimate the cutoff from the data and apply both parametric (local linear) and nonparametric (rdrobust) approaches.

## 2. R Code

```r
# Load required libraries
if (!require("rdrobust")) install.packages("rdrobust", repos="https://cran.r-project.org")
if (!require("rddensity")) install.packages("rddensity", repos="https://cran.r-project.org")
library(rdrobust)
library(rddensity)

# Read data
df <- read.csv("experiments/exp_b/data/s91_data.csv")

cat("=== Data Overview ===\n")
str(df)
summary(df)

# Identify the cutoff
# treated=1 when running_var is below the cutoff (VLBW = low birth weight)
# Let's find the cutoff by examining the boundary between treated and untreated
cat("\n=== Identifying the Cutoff ===\n")
max_treated <- max(df$running_var[df$treated == 1])
min_untreated <- min(df$running_var[df$treated == 0])
cat("Max running_var among treated:", max_treated, "\n")
cat("Min running_var among untreated:", min_untreated, "\n")
cutoff <- (max_treated + min_untreated) / 2
cat("Estimated cutoff:", cutoff, "\n")

# Check if treatment is sharp
# Treatment should be: treated = 1 if running_var < cutoff
sharp_check <- all(df$treated == as.integer(df$running_var < cutoff))
cat("Sharp RDD confirmed:", sharp_check, "\n")

# If not perfectly sharp, try different cutoff values
if (!sharp_check) {
  # Try common cutoffs
  for (c in c(0.5, 0.45, 0.4, 0.3)) {
    check <- mean(df$treated == as.integer(df$running_var < c))
    cat("Cutoff =", c, "-> agreement:", check, "\n")
    if (check > 0.99) { cutoff <- c; break }
  }
}

# Center the running variable at the cutoff
df$X <- df$running_var - cutoff

cat("\n=== Distribution Around Cutoff ===\n")
cat("N treated:", sum(df$treated), "\n")
cat("N control:", sum(df$treated == 0), "\n")
cat("N near cutoff:", sum(df$near_cutoff), "\n")

# ========================================
# Main Analysis: rdrobust (nonparametric)
# ========================================
cat("\n=== Main RDD Estimate (rdrobust) ===\n")
rd_main <- rdrobust(y = df$y, x = df$X, c = 0)
summary(rd_main)

cat("\nRDD Treatment Effect Estimate:", rd_main$coef[1], "\n")
cat("Robust 95% CI: [", rd_main$ci[3,1], ",", rd_main$ci[3,2], "]\n")
cat("Robust p-value:", rd_main$pv[3], "\n")
cat("Effective N left:", rd_main$N_h[1], " right:", rd_main$N_h[2], "\n")
cat("Bandwidth:", rd_main$bws[1,1], "\n")

# ========================================
# Robustness 1: Different kernel
# ========================================
cat("\n=== Robustness: Uniform Kernel ===\n")
rd_uniform <- rdrobust(y = df$y, x = df$X, c = 0, kernel = "uniform")
summary(rd_uniform)

# ========================================
# Robustness 2: Different bandwidth selection
# ========================================
cat("\n=== Robustness: MSE-Two Bandwidth ===\n")
rd_msetwo <- rdrobust(y = df$y, x = df$X, c = 0, bwselect = "msetwo")
summary(rd_msetwo)

# ========================================
# Robustness 3: Half and double bandwidth
# ========================================
cat("\n=== Robustness: Half Bandwidth ===\n")
rd_half <- rdrobust(y = df$y, x = df$X, c = 0, h = rd_main$bws[1,1] / 2)
summary(rd_half)

cat("\n=== Robustness: Double Bandwidth ===\n")
rd_double <- rdrobust(y = df$y, x = df$X, c = 0, h = rd_main$bws[1,1] * 2)
summary(rd_double)

# ========================================
# Robustness 4: Parametric local linear regression
# ========================================
cat("\n=== Robustness: Parametric Local Linear ===\n")
bw <- rd_main$bws[1,1]
df_local <- df[abs(df$X) <= bw, ]
lm_local <- lm(y ~ treated * X, data = df_local)
cat("Parametric estimate within optimal bandwidth:\n")
print(summary(lm_local))
cat("\nTreatment coefficient:", coef(lm_local)["treated"], "\n")

# ========================================
# Robustness 5: Quadratic specification
# ========================================
cat("\n=== Robustness: Local Quadratic (rdrobust p=2) ===\n")
rd_quad <- rdrobust(y = df$y, x = df$X, c = 0, p = 2)
summary(rd_quad)

# ========================================
# McCrary Density Test (Manipulation Test)
# ========================================
cat("\n=== McCrary Density Test (Manipulation Check) ===\n")
density_test <- rddensity(X = df$X, c = 0)
summary(density_test)
cat("Density test p-value:", density_test$test$p_jk, "\n")
cat("(If p > 0.05, no evidence of manipulation at the cutoff)\n")

# ========================================
# Summary Table
# ========================================
cat("\n=== SUMMARY OF ALL ESTIMATES ===\n")
cat(sprintf("%-30s %10s %10s %10s\n", "Specification", "Estimate", "SE", "p-value"))
cat(paste(rep("-", 62), collapse=""), "\n")
cat(sprintf("%-30s %10.4f %10.4f %10.4f\n", "Main (MSE-opt, triangular)", 
            rd_main$coef[1], rd_main$se[3], rd_main$pv[3]))
cat(sprintf("%-30s %10.4f %10.4f %10.4f\n", "Uniform kernel", 
            rd_uniform$coef[1], rd_uniform$se[3], rd_uniform$pv[3]))
cat(sprintf("%-30s %10.4f %10.4f %10.4f\n", "MSE-Two bandwidth", 
            rd_msetwo$coef[1], rd_msetwo$se[3], rd_msetwo$pv[3]))
cat(sprintf("%-30s %10.4f %10.4f %10.4f\n", "Half bandwidth", 
            rd_half$coef[1], rd_half$se[3], rd_half$pv[3]))
cat(sprintf("%-30s %10.4f %10.4f %10.4f\n", "Double bandwidth", 
            rd_double$coef[1], rd_double$se[3], rd_double$pv[3]))
cat(sprintf("%-30s %10.4f %10.4f %10.4f\n", "Local quadratic (p=2)", 
            rd_quad$coef[1], rd_quad$se[3], rd_quad$pv[3]))
cat(sprintf("%-30s %10.4f %10.4f %10.4f\n", "Parametric local linear", 
            coef(lm_local)["treated"], summary(lm_local)$coefficients["treated","Std. Error"],
            summary(lm_local)$coefficients["treated","Pr(>|t|)"]))
```

## 3. Expected Findings

**Expected sign:** **Positive** — Being classified as VLBW (treated=1, below the threshold) is expected to be associated with **higher** log neonatal mortality. Infants just below the VLBW threshold have slightly lower birth weights, and despite potentially receiving additional medical attention due to the classification, the underlying health vulnerability dominates.

However, there is an important competing mechanism: VLBW classification triggers additional medical interventions, monitoring, and resource allocation (e.g., NICU placement, specialist care). This could create a **negative** discontinuity — meaning VLBW classification actually *reduces* mortality by channeling extra care to these infants. This is the Almond et al. (2010, QJE) finding, where mortality is lower just below the VLBW cutoff due to the additional treatment.

**Expected magnitude:** Given the normalized running variable and log mortality outcome, I expect a discontinuity on the order of **0.1–0.5 in log points** (roughly 10–50% change in mortality). The sign could go either way depending on how the DGP was constructed, but the classic empirical finding suggests a **negative** effect (VLBW classification reduces mortality through additional care), with magnitude around 0.2–0.4 log points.

**Density test:** I expect no evidence of manipulation (p > 0.05) since birth weight near the threshold is plausibly random, supporting the RDD validity.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: Exploit the discontinuity at the birth weight threshold for classification.
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: Crossing the threshold for very-low-birth-weight classification increases neonatal mortality.
